elements.text: Explosion of the center wing fuel tank (CWT)
Ignition of the flammable fuel/air mixture in the CWT
Short circuit outside of the CWT allowing excessive voltage to enter through FQIS wiring
Design and certification concept that fuel tank explosions could be prevented solely by precluding all ignition sources
Design and certification of the Boeing 747 with heat sources located beneath the CWT
Lack of means to reduce heat transferred into the CWT
Lack of means to render the fuel vapor in the tank nonflammable
Flight crew was properly certificated and qualified
No evidence of preexisting medical or behavioral conditions affecting crew performance
Airplane was certificated, equipped, and dispatched in accordance with regulations
No significant meteorological conditions disrupted the flight
In-flight breakup was not initiated by preexisting structural failure
In-flight breakup was not initiated by a bomb or missile strike
Fuel/air vapor in the CWT ullage was flammable at the time of the accident
Fuel/air explosion capable of generating sufficient internal pressure to break apart the tank
Witness observations of light streaks were not related to a missile
Witness observations of fireballs were of burning wreckage
In-flight breakup was initiated by a fuel/air explosion in the CWT
Boeing’s design practice permitting unbonded parts <3 inches may not provide adequate protection against static electricity ignition hazards
Unlikely that vapor was ignited by lightning, missile, explosive, auto ignition, fire migration, engine failure, pump malfunction, or static electricity
EM interference from external radio sources did not produce enough energy to ignite vapor
EM interference from personal electronic devices played no role
Unlikely that EM interference from aircraft system wiring played a role
Existing standards for wire separation may not provide adequate protection against short circuit damage
Short circuit producing excess voltage transferred to FQIS wiring is the most likely source of ignition energy
Silver-sulfide deposits on FQIS components pose a risk for ignition
Ignition energy most likely entered CWT through FQIS wiring
Failure modes and effects analyses should not be relied upon as sole means of demonstrating fuel tank safety
Fuel tank design philosophy relying solely on elimination of ignition sources is fundamentally flawed
Operating airplanes with flammable fuel/air mixtures presents an avoidable risk
Placement of heat-generating equipment under fuel tank increases time operating with flammable mixture
Wiring system condition was not atypical and maintenance was in accordance with practices
Insufficient attention paid to aircraft electrical wiring condition
FAA’s Aging Transport Non-Structural Systems Plan issues are important safety issues
